en: Preface to the Record of the Carving and Explanation of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*:
Now, the practice of seeking rebirth in the Land of Bliss has been praised by all the sages and revered by the multitude of worthies.

For this reason, Mañjuśrī and Maitreya vowed to be born there, while Vasubandhu and Nāgārjuna pledged to go thither. If even such holy ones acted thus, how much more so should those of us who are ignorant and deluded? During the Liu Song dynasty...
Later, the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra retranslated this sūtra, after which various schools flourished with elegant expositions.
Yet, as for our Great Master of Zhongnan—who stands solemnly as a model for both ancient and modern times—it goes without saying that he established his own school;
but among all those who have spoken from the golden mouth or through wooden tongues, who can compare to Zen Master Zhi? His explanation states: "This..."

The sutra takes mental contemplation as its primary principle and the true mark (*dharmatā*) as its essence. Zhiyi of the Four Clarifications said: "By relying on an object to contemplate the Buddha, the marks of the Buddha become manifest.
The entire mind is the Buddha; the entire Buddha is the mind. All day long one contemplates the mind; all day long one contemplates the Buddha.
While these words are indeed excellent, they are like discarding the skill of adapting to the moment; I do not accept them. Recently, some people have praised [this view].
If one can achieve buddha-remembrance through the mind alone, what need is there for other Buddhas? Is it not difficult to speak of this, and would it not be considered impudent?
It is merely like attempting to leap over the North Sea while clutching Mount Tai. Furthermore, some people say that the Great Vow consists in the invocation of the Name.
These are merely provisional expedients; they are not to be relied upon. How grave indeed is this doctrine!
It is violent and tyrannical, slandering the words of the Sage by taking the right for wrong and the wrong for right. It indulges in deceptive rhetoric and treats the multitude with contempt.

If this can be tolerated, what cannot be tolerated? Master Fǎcóng of the Tang dynasty was the first to compose the *Commentary on the Sūtra of Contemplation* (Guānjīng shùjì) according to the Tiantai tradition.
Its prose is concise yet its principles are clear; its diction is brief yet its matters are complete.
It even draws upon my own discourse on Zhongnan. Finally, Baoyun and Siming followed in succession, flourishing like luxuriant growth.
Yet, because Master Cong’s record had already been submerged and lost in distant lands, it caused Baoyun and Siming to remain unaware that such a text existed within this world.
In the past, Master Zhen of Saimon traveled across the sea upon a raft and obtained this record, returning with it to Kaiyuan Temple.
Yet he still concealed it within a famous mountain and unrolled it in a stone chamber; thus, it remained absent from the human world for a long time indeed.
I have explored the golden tablets at famous mountains and obtained this scripture from a stone chamber.

Now, in this year of Yimao (1475), I am about to have it carved into printing blocks to show it to the great assembly. Indeed, this record is not merely a discourse on the "harp and flute" harmony between the wise;
it shall also serve as wings for those who travel through our Zhongnan Mountains. For this reason, Master Liangzhong once recorded four [sections].
A Postscript: I have used this record to explain that commentary. Thus, it is now for the scholars of Zhongnan.

How could it be abandoned? How could it be abandoned? I prostrate myself in hope that you will analyze the difficult and the easy, and refute deceptive言辞 (words/phrases), so that this simpleton and ignorant one may leave this thorny forest and roam beneath those jade trees. Would this not be a profound blessing? Thus, I have written this preface.
Record of the Commentary on the Sūtra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life,
compiled by the śramaṇa Bai-pin Yashan of Nanxi at Yuanshan in Wuyang, in the year of Longji (Yimao),
the twenty-first year of the Enkyō era (November).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Fǎcóng.

In explaining the text of the commentary, it is divided into two main sections: first, a general clarification of the differences between the two lands regarding their physical environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*);

second, from the passage "However, because the causes for transformation were gradual" onwards, a specific explanation of the purpose for which this sutra was brought forth. The first section is further divided into three parts: namely, the Dharma-explanation, the analogy, and the application of the analogy to the Dharma.

Second, first clarifying the differences between the two lands and their two fruits; next, from "Truly, it is because the mind divides into defilement and purity" onwards, distinguishing the differences in the cultivation of causes for the two lands.
This section has two parts: first, the initial two lines clarify the differences in the dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) of the two lands;

second, from "womb and prison" onwards, discussing how the two fruits of the dependent and the primary (*adhiṣṭhāna*) differ in each land. This [second part] also has two sections: the first line generally clarifies both lands.
The next two phrases, "depending upon suffering" and "joy," clarify the purity and defilement of the two lands.
Now, regarding the phrase "land of joy" (*sukhāvatī*): the word "now" (*fu*) marks the beginning of the discourse; "land of joy" refers to the Pure Land of Shared Residence (*sahabhū-sukhāvatī*).
"Joy" is because that land lacks the three evil realms (*durgati*), such that both types of retribution are joyful. "Land" (*bang*) refers to the boundaries of a pure country.

Furthermore, as for "joy," there are ponds with eight flowing streams where the sand is made of vajra; the ground wells up with the seven treasures interspersed with lapis lazuli, and rows of jewel-trees stand in order.

Birds and winds preach the Dharma; these two forms of retribution are free from suffering. One constantly hears the Mahāyāna, and those of the three grades of rebirth are born amidst blossoming flowers to behold the Buddha.
Both the primary and secondary environments proclaim the teachings, and all praise the Triple Gem—this is called the realm of joy. As for the realm of suffering, it is the Land of Common Abode.
The suffering of the defiled land refers to the Sahā world, where various evils coexist and the five turbidities and eight sufferings sear one day and night.
The ten evil karmas flourish and the cycle of rebirth never ceases; the fruits of sagehood remain unattained as one is ensnared by the three delusions.

Boundless in birth and death, one has not yet escaped and must endure the three poisons; therefore, it is called suffering. Thus, there are the three sufferings and the eight sufferings within this realm.
Because this Sahā world has boundaries, it is called a "realm" (*kṣetra*). Regarding "gold and jewels," those dwelling in the Pure Land all have their surroundings adorned with jewels.

Regarding "mud and sand," the impure lands shared by ordinary beings consist entirely of grit and pebbles. The above concludes the explanation of the environmental fruits (*niśraya-phala*) of the two lands.

Next, the two lines clarify the environmental and personal retributions (*niśraya-sambhoga* and *sambhoga-phala*) of the two lands. Regarding "wombs and prisons": in this land, the personal retribution consists of remaining in the womb for ten months.
The moon suffers from various colds and fevers; the meaning of the body-consciousness finding no joy is like being in a womb or a prison.

Regarding the "lotus pond," both those newly born and those long-established through transformation in the Pure Land dwell within jeweled ponds, where they cultivate causes and encounter conditions to produce flowers and fruits.

Regarding the "thorn forest," this refers to the thorny and evil environments of this world, where the external retribution is like a forest of thorns. "Jade trees" refers to precious trees; in the Pure Land, there are seven [kinds].
The rows of trees are all made of jewels; some have roots of gold, stems of purple-gold, branches of white silver, twigs of agate, leaves of coral, flowers of white jade, and fruits of pearls.
Thus, the forty-nine rows of trees—seven times seven—are all jeweled trees. This concludes the explanation of the two lands and their two fruits. Next:
The following four lines distinguish the differences in the cultivation of causes for the two lands: "It is truly due to the division of the mind into defilement and purity" is indeed the reality.

Because of this defilement and purity, the mind is divided into two. It is solely because when the mind is pure and one practices goodness, one ascends to the Land of Bliss, with its wondrous jeweled grounds, jeweled ponds, and jade trees;
whereas when the mind has defilement and one practices evil, one sinks into the realm of suffering, the mire.

Regarding the coarse boundary of the sand-jujube grove, the second section of the analogy has two parts. First, the initial phrase uses the purity of the Buddha-land’s cause and effect as an analogy, stating that "if the form is upright, the shadow is straight.
Second, the subsequent phrase uses this world’s cause and effect as an analogy; because the mind is defiled, the fruit is suffering, hence it says, "if the source is turbid, the flow is murky.

Third, regarding the application [of the analogy] below, there are two parts: first, clarifying the cause and effect of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment); next, beginning with "I vow to see... [the text continues].
This clarifies the cause and effect of the primary retribution (*vipāka*). The text states:

"Therefore, know that those who wish to be born in the Pure Land" encourages the people of this land to cultivate the *āśraya-phala* (the fruit of the environment) of that land, which is the purely pure dwelling place. Next, it necessarily encourages those with affinity in this land to cultivate the cause and effect of the wondrous land.
The following two lines clarify the primary retribution: "I vow to see the World-Honored One" means that seeing the Buddha is the essential practice for realizing the fruit of Sukhāvatī.
Pure karma is the cultivation of causes; the three types of pure karma will be explained below in the text itself.
Now, regarding the second section, which specifically clarifies the purpose for which this sutra has come, it is divided into three parts: first, a general clarification of the sutra’s intent;

second, a specific explanation of the title starting from "The mental contemplation of this sutra"; and third, the interpretation according to the text, which is further divided into three sections. Below, the explanation follows the text.

The initial text is divided into three parts: first, the clarification of the three intentions; second, from "Next, setting aside the [previous]... onwards, the detailed exposition of the main body of the teaching, clarifying the general principles of contemplation and summarizing the intent of the sutra;
third, from "It may be called subtle practice... onwards, the concluding praise.

The first section has three parts: first, the introduction; second, from "The Great Sage" onwards, the exposition of the main teaching; third, from "Causing those in the vulgar world who have a karmic affinity" onwards, the praise for the circulation [of the text].
Regarding the introduction, it consists of two parts: the *samyak-pratyaya* (evidence of faith) and the *nidāna* (circumstances of the origin). "Ran" (然) means "it is thus.

"Transformation" (*hua*) refers to the Buddha appearing in the world to deliver sentient beings and proclaiming the four kinds of eloquence; this is termed "transformation. "Cause" (*yin*) refers to sentient beings possessing the capacity as the cause for the event.

Regarding the various manifestations of the Buddhas' transformative activities, three are prior and one is subsequent; these constitute the "matter" (vastu). Furthermore, within the general introduction (*nidāna*), five of the six phrases are also termed "matter.

As for the "gradual" (*anupūrva*), it refers to adapting the Dharma to the capacities of sentient beings; through gradual and sudden cultivation, two types of persons realize two kinds of fruits—those that resemble the Great and Small Vehicles, yet are not truly so.
"Teaching" (*śāsana*) refers to the gates of the expressive doctrine, which are of four distinct types: namely, the *piṭaka*, the *sāmānya*, the *viśeṣa*, and the [unspecified fourth].
"Yuan" (Complete) refers to the "Sequence of the Arising of Conditions" (*yuanxing xia*) below; this is the introductory section concerning the manifestation of the two conditions of good and evil.
King Ajātaśatru represents evil, for he committed two perversions by killing his father and harming his mother; thus he is called a "perpetrator of parricide.

Vaidehī represents good, as she gave rise to a compassionate plea—where "ai" (哀) signifies grief—and made her request to the King, which was a universal plea including both herself and her followers, as well as the sentient beings of future generations.

Therefore, it says, "Next, the Great Sage [is entreated with] a piteous plea," which clarifies the intent of the orthodox teaching (*zhengzong*). "Great Sage" (*dàshèng*) is a title for the Ultimate Honored One;
because his own practice has reached fruition, he has exhausted the source and perfected nature, and he is fully endowed with wisdom and severance, he is called the "Great Sage.

"Great" (*dà*) has the meaning of "encompassing," as it encompasses the three, five, seven, and nine [aspects]; thus he is called the Great Sage. "Sage" (*shèng*) means "correctness"; the three bodies are equally realized therein.

His responses are necessarily manifested through wisdom that is coextensive with the Dharma-realm; he exhausts the source of both good and evil, such that his function is nowhere not ultimate, his illumination is nowhere not pervasive, and his penetrating insight leaves nothing behind, for he understands all things.
Therefore, he is called a Sage. The Śūraṅgama Samādhi encompasses everything without exception;

as a mirror for the three wheels, he discerns the capacities of beings and bestows medicine through the four analytical eloquences. He provides medicine according to the ailment, enabling them to take it and practice it; therefore, he is called a Great Sage.

"Chui" (垂) refers to the downward-reaching reflection; "Lin" (臨) means to respond to the capacities of beings across the ten realms. "Ci" (慈) refers to the three types of compassion, wherein the Dharma and sentient beings rejoice together.
"Jingji" (乘機) refers to the two wheels of body and mind. "Jianji" (鑒機) means to discern capacities through vision that penetrates both the Great and Small Vehicles, benefiting all.

"Yanfa" (演法) refers to the wheel of speech, expounding the four teachings of the Half and Full [Vehicles]. "Yaoyue" (曜) refers to light, which illuminates and manifests reflections. "Yuxiang" (玉相) refers to the emission of white [light].
The "hair-mark" (*ūrṇā-kośa*) pervades the worlds of the ten directions because its radiant golden-hued marks are like variegated colors.
The "precious terrace" (*ratna-pīṭha*) refers to the golden terrace; that which it symbolizes is called "auspicious. It is called "broad" because the light illuminates the ten directions.

It is called "manifesting" because it appears in all lands. It is called "precious" because all nations consist of jewels. It is called a "domain" (*viṣaya*) because it demarcates the realms of the Buddhas; this is the essential meaning.

Regarding the "returner": although Vaidehī beheld that all the lands possessed radiance, her spiritual capacity (*indriya*) was directed toward the Pure Land; therefore, she said, "I vow to be born in the presence of Amitābha Buddha.
As for the "three exhortations for the vulgar of the final age," this praises the meaning of the circulation [of the teaching].

"The vulgar of the final age" refers to sentient beings with karmic affinities during the period of the Semblance Dharma and the Final Age, who, through the mutual resonance of cause and response, shall all go according to their karma—that is, they shall attain birth in the present time.
People follow and revere this because of it. This wondrous contemplation consists of the sixteen contemplations;
when a single thought arises, the environment and its inhabitants appear clearly, yet they are entirely complete as emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way.
Because the three aspects are mutually identical, perfectly interfused, and sovereign—neither identical nor different—it is called the wondrous contemplation.

Next, regarding the "Setting Sun" section, which establishes the main body of the text in detail: the setting sun corresponds to the first visualization; the great water freezing into ice corresponds to the visualization of water;

the lapis lazuli ground corresponds to the third visualization (which also incorporates the element of water); the chanting of precious leaves corresponds to the fourth visualization of the trees and the seventh visualization of the flower seats;
the celestial music corresponds to the sixth visualization; and the rippling golden channels correspond to the fifth visualization of the ponds.
Contemplating the brief resonance that accords with the sound is the eighth contemplation; contemplating the fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) and so forth is the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth;

the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the mark of the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa) and so forth is the ninth; the meaning of the True Body encompasses the eighth, the universal, and the miscellaneous three contemplations;
and as for closing the eyes and so forth, these refer to the final three contemplations, whereby those of the three grades and nine ranks ascend the lotus pedestal to attain rebirth.
"Clouds soaring high and patterns formed" refers to receiving birth in the Pure Land; "seals destroyed" refers to the cessation of the five aggregates (skandhas) in this world.

"Golden lotuses" are the vehicles of the three grades of merit and retribution. "Traversing horizontally as one goes" means cutting across the three delusions and attaining birth in the upper, middle, or lower grades.

These delusions—view-delusion, thought-delusion, dust-and-sand delusion, and ignorance—are the three maladies that cause one to be perpetually alarmed; "galloping toward the meaning" means to proceed immediately.
The Venerable Yeshu Yi recited these verses: "Pure and radiant, free from all dust and defilement, born by transformation from a lotus flower as father and mother;
having practiced the Way for ten kalpas, he manifested birth in Jambudvīpa to undergo manifold sufferings. Through a single lifetime of ascetic practice, he transcends a thousand kalpas;
forever departing Saṃsāra, he returns to the Pure Land. Having passed beyond the five and eight sufferings of this land, he is forever freed from impurity."
Because one attains non-retrogression regarding the single realm, it is called "long-lasting alarm.
This may be described as the subtle practice that eliminates the three lower fetters. The practitioner’s three kinds of pure karma are the marvelous contemplation of the ultimate Way;
because these sixteen contemplations are perfectly integrated and sovereign—being three while being one—it is called "marvelous. Thus, through the cultivation of causes, one attains the fruit.
Because one has come from here to reach that [state], it is called the "Path of Arrival" (*prāptimārga*). "Path" (*mārga*) signifies that which enables passage to what is to be reached.

Although there are many types of karmic activities, taking mental contemplation as the essential technique is paramount. When a single thought-moment arises, the Pure Land is perfectly manifest; its essence remains as it was, unconditioned.

It is said that even subtle practices consist of the three contemplations within a single mind. Within emptiness, provisionality, and the middle way, although subject and object are distinguished, they mutually illuminate one another beyond conceptual thought.

The essential point of deliberating upon the realm lies in the source of the mind; this is the merit of contemplation. Transversally pervasive and vertically exhaustive, it is equal and without duality.

Because the perfection of the three virtues as the fruit arises from the fulfillment of the three contemplations through the principle of the mind's essence, it is called "the essential art of the ultimate Way."

This section, "Contemplation of the Mind," is the second part [of the treatise] and consists of two sub-sections: first, a brief explanation, and second, a detailed exposition. The brief explanation has two parts: first, it clarifies the essential doctrine and substance;

second, from the words "That which is spoken of... onwards, it provides a concise commentary on the title of the sutra. By citing the primary retribution (the Buddha) to encompass the secondary fruits (the environment), the contemplation of the True Body is used to subsume the preceding eight gates.
By mentioning the Transformation Lord (Amitābha) to include his retinue, the power of the transformer is shown to encompass that which is transformed.

Regarding the transformation and liberation of sentient beings with whom there is a karmic affinity, the term "Buddha" encompasses all contemplations and signifies that the Buddha’s activity is universal.

This refers to both the Buddha who speaks and the Buddha who is spoken of. The Buddha as the transformative master is the Capable Benevolent One (Śākyamuni), while the Buddha who is the object of contemplation is Amitābha, who appears in the Ninth Contemplation.

When the subject and object are explained in conjunction, this constitutes the Sixteen Contemplations. The land where they dwell corresponds to the preceding seven contemplations, and the sentient beings who are transformed constitute the objective capacity.
Because it subsumes the latter five contemplations, a single word of the Buddha encompasses both subject and object, fully possessing all sixteen aspects;
as these are all the Buddha’s own teaching, his discourse is thus complete.

Next is the extensive explanation of the five meanings, which is twofold: first, the presentation and enumeration, and second, the explanation according to the text. Regarding the name, essence, and so forth of this sutra:

This sutra is titled according to its person; its essence is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*); its central tenet is the mental contemplation of the Pure Land; its function is the production of goodness and the extinction of evil;
and its pedagogical characteristic is the elucidation of the full teaching in contrast to the half-teaching.

Next, the explanation of the five meanings is divided into five sections. First, the explanation of the name is divided into two parts: first, the general explanation, and second, the specific explanation. The text for these is further divided into two: first, the explanation, and second, the concluding praise.

The first of these (the general explanation) is divided into three parts: first, the general explanation of "one transformation" (*eka-vikāra*); second, the explanation in relation to "one sūtra"; and third, the explanation in relation to "one character.

Regarding the first of these (the general explanation), there are two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the conclusion. The general explanation consists of the resolution of both the general and the specific; generally, "sūtra" refers to the dharmas of sound and form as the sūtra, while specifically...

There are seven [types], namely: three single [categories], three pairs, and one complete set, distinguished as follows. Regarding the single person: such as the *Sūtra of the Householder Trapusa* and the *Sūtra of Prince Sudāna*.
Regarding the single dharma: such as the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and so forth. Regarding the single simile:
these three are the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, the *Śuṣkavṛkṣa-sūtra*, and the *Loutan-jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra). Alternatively, there are those named after both person and dharma, such as...

In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the title is based on the Dharma and the parable; in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is based on the person and the parable; and in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, it is based on the person, the Dharma, and the parable.

These three constitute the "redundant" (or composite) titles. Alternatively, as in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the title "Mahāvaipulya Buddha-avataṃsaka" combines the person, the Dharma, and the parable—this is the "triple" [title].
Regarding the distinctions among the practices from one up to the infinite: if one cultivates a single practice, that is "one."
Contemplating the Tathāgata’s practice involves two practices: the cultivation of form and mind, and meditative concentration and wisdom;
three practices: the three truths and the three contemplations; four practices: the four truths and the four immeasurables; five practices: the cultivation of the five eyes and the five faculties;
six practices: the six perfections; seven practices: the seven factors of enlightenment; eight practices: the eightfold noble path; nine practices: the nine dharma-realms and the nine...
The ten practices of the Great Dhyāna are the ten vehicles of contemplative methods (*daśayāna-dhyāna*) and the ten dharma-realms (*daśadhātu*).

Within each of the four teachings (*caturvidha-śāsana*), there are four gates (*catvāro dvārāḥ*), and within each gate, all practices are fully present; thus they are called "immeasurable practices. Although these practices are numerous, they all converge upon the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the four virtues (*caturguṇa*).

This constitutes the sixteen gates resulting from the fourfold application of the four [teachings]. Specifically, the *zàng* (Tripiṭaka) teaching has the four gates of birth-and-death (*utpādanirodha*), while the *tōng* (Shared) teaching...
Regarding the four gates of non-arising, distinct teaching, immeasurable perfect teaching, and unconditioned arising-and-ceasing:

these are existence, emptiness, both existence and emptiness, and neither existence nor emptiness. The three teachings are likewise so. The first two teachings accord with the partial truth of reality;

the latter two accord with the perfect middle-way principle. Existence, sequence, non-sequence, the distinct, and the perfect—these are the distinct principles. The same principle follows the gate; the principle varies according to the name.

Thus, they are called "distinct. This refers to the conclusion regarding a single period of transformation. That is, during the Buddha’s appearance in the world, throughout his entire career of universal transformation, there are five flavors of teaching.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, the flavor of milk, there are the distinct and the perfect [teachings], comprising eight gates. In the *Āgama*, the flavor of curd, there are the four gates of the Tripitaka Teaching.

In the Vaipulya, the flavor of fresh butter, there are the four teachings, totaling sixteen gates. In the Prajñāpāramitā, the flavor of matured butter, there are the common, distinct, and perfect [teachings], totaling ten [gates].

Regarding the two gates: the *Lotus Sūtra* is the flavor of the finest cream (*tīrāma*). It exclusively reveals and clarifies the perfect [teaching] through four gates, opening up the previous four flavors and bringing them all into the cream-flavor.

Wisdom and severance are fully perfected, and the principle is exhausted in the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Next, concerning the general and specific aspects of the verbal teachings of this single sūtra:

the Buddha’s preaching is the teaching; the teaching is the means of expression (*vyañjana*). Practice is that which is practiced; the principle is that which is expressed (*artha*). These three—teaching, practice, and principle—are the causes cultivated through cultivation.
Because the wisdom of the exhaustion of delusions at the ultimate fruit is luminous, three dharmas are required. Following the Buddha, there is the summary of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

This section has two parts: first, the summary of the praise; second, using a small case to illustrate the great. First, the Dharma-body corresponds to principle (*tattva*), Prajñā corresponds to teaching (*śāsana*), and Liberation corresponds to practice (*caryā*).

All are realized through the cultivation of the three teachings, practices, and principles via the single mind and the threefold contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). Thus, the three bodies are harmoniously integrated and non-dual; emptiness is precisely...
Prajñā is itself provisional, and liberation is itself the Dharmakāya. Since this is true for the names [of these concepts], it must likewise apply to the entirety of the sutra;
thus, the three contemplations (trivipaśyanā) must be fully present. Next, regarding even a single character, let us take a few examples to illustrate the many:

within the single character "form" (rūpa), the meaning of the three contemplations is established. Therefore, the Sutra says: "All dharmas tend toward form; there is no tending beyond form. Within "form," nothing can be apprehended.
How is it that when there is neither coming nor going, the three contemplations are fully realized within the provisional emptiness?
Next, the text is explained in detail in four parts: first, the Buddha; second, the three contemplations; third, the four immeasurables; and fourth, Amitāyus.
The Buddha has six aspects, which correspond to the meaning of the "six identities. First is the *Li-ji Fo* (Buddha in Principle). The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"All sentient beings are the precious storehouse within the Mahāyāna house and the pearl on the forehead. This is explained at length in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary*.

Regarding the ten metaphors of the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, there are differences between the two versions; when cited in various texts, some refer to it as the "Buddha-garbha" (*Fo-zang*), which is merely a matter of linguistic convenience. Text.
In the Vaipulya *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, a single-fascicle scripture, the Buddha spoke for the sake of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
Although the text contains ten points in meaning, it appears as nine, because the first two sections share a single meaning. The initial section states:
"With my Buddha-eye, I observe that within the afflictions of all sentient beings, there exists Buddha-wisdom and the body of a Tathāgata, sitting cross-legged."
Sitting cross-legged, majestic and unmoving. Good son, it is like using the divine eye to observe a flower that has not yet blossomed;
once the withered petals have been removed, the Tathāgata within becomes manifest. The Buddha’s vision of sentient beings is also like this.

The following nine similes comprise nine sections in total, each consisting of both prose and verse in four or five lines. Now, I shall briefly cite the essentials and combine them with what precedes.
The first simile states: "For example, it is like a withered and decaying flower that has not yet blossomed; one with the divine eye perceives the Tathāgata’s body as being free from defilement.
The second states: "For example, it is like a tree laden with honey surrounded by immeasurable bees;

one who employs skillful means first removes the swarm of bees. The third states: "For example, it is like all varieties of fine grain whose husks have not yet been removed or winnowed, [and which would be useless] to the poor."
4. It is like regarding something as base and thus fit to be discarded;

yet it is said that gold, though hidden within impurity so that none can see it, is perceived by one with the divine eye (divyacakṣus), who then informs the multitude. 5. It is like a poor man’s house containing a treasury of precious jewels;
the master neither knows nor sees the treasure, nor can he speak of it. 6. It is like the interior of an *āmra* fruit.
7. It is said: "In truth, if one does not destroy the seed planted in the great earth, it will surely become a king of great trees.
8. It is said: "For example, it is like carrying a golden image to another region wrapped in filthy rags and discarding it in a wilderness.
9. It is said: "For example, it is like a poor woman whose appearance is exceedingly ugly, yet who carries a child of noble marks destined to become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*)."
For example, it is like a great smith casting immeasurable images of pure gold. The fool, looking from the outside, sees only scorched black earth;
yet within that earth lies the Buddha-nature. This serves as a metaphor for two things: first, the "name" (nāman), which refers to generating the Mahayana mind by taking the principle as its object;

second, the "practice" (pratipatti), which refers to cultivating the inconceivable ten dharma-attainments through the three contemplations until one attains unimpeded penetration. Fourth is the stage of "semblance," which refers to the mutual functioning of the six sense faculties.
The faith of the Bodhisattva who has resolved upon the Great Mind marks the long parting from the ocean of suffering within the wheel of the triple world.

The five stages of partial realization refer to the forty-one positions: the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment. First, the text clarifies the three virtues; next, from "This principle... onwards, it praises the non-duality of their essence.

Next, regarding "although there are five immediate [retributions]" (*pañcānantarya*), the principle is that this is the Vimuktikāya (Liberation Body). As for the five immediate retributions: first, immediacy of receiving retribution (receiving retribution upon casting off the body);

second, immediacy of suffering (because there is no pleasure in between); third, immediacy of time (being fixed at one kalpa); fourth, immediacy of life (because there is no interruption in between); fifth, immediacy of form...
In the Avīci Hell (where their bodies fill eighty thousand *yojanas*), whether one person or many people occupy that same space, they do not obstruct one another, yet all are completely pervasive;

"Next, this principle is manifest" praises the essence of the principle as being eternally equal, non-dual, and free from the distinctions of existence and non-existence, high and low; it is the primordial principle of the awakened nature (*bodhata*).

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that for one hundred and eighty kalpas, [beings] first cited two sūtras and did not hear the names [of the teaching] for many kalpas. Subsequently, when a Buddha appeared in the world, through the emergence of the cause capable of explaining it, they were able to hear it;
having heard the teaching, they sought its expression and practiced until they attained the principle. Therefore, it is said that "the nectar-gate is opened."
Each and every gate is itself the teaching; since ambrosia (*amṛta*) is the principle, when Sudatta heard its name, the hairs on his body all stood on end.

During the middle watch of the night, he arose and addressed his kinsmen: "Virtuous ones, you should rise quickly;

"Is it not that he wishes to invite King Māgadha? Why is there such unrest as this? The elder replied: "No, householder. Tomorrow..."
He requested the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Dharma King. When the elder Sudatta first heard the name of the Buddha, the hairs on his body all stood on end.
He immediately asked, "What is meant by 'Buddha'? The elder replied, "Have you not heard? In the city of Kapilavastu, there is a son of the Śākyas named Siddhārtha, of the Gautama clan.
His father’s name is Śuddhodana... [and so forth], until he eventually renounced his home and departed.
Without a teacher, he attained self-awakening to *sambodhi*. With greed, hatred, and delusion exhausted, he abides eternally and unchangingly;

Furthermore, because he is fully endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), the five knowledges (*pañcajñāna*), the samādhis, great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and the three foundations of mindfulness (*trismṛtyupasthāna*), he is called a Buddha. Sudatta said, "Excellent, Great Being! As for the one you call the Buddha, his merit is unsurpassed; where is he now?
The elder replied, "He is currently here in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery at Rājagṛha.
At that time, Sudatta single-mindedly called to mind all the merits of the Buddha—the ten powers, the fearlessnesses (and so forth), up to the three bases of mindfulness.

Fearlessness is the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), which is the fruit;

the three virtues consist of contemplating the form-body as provisional, contemplating the dharma-gate body as empty, and contemplating the reality-body (dharmatākāya) as the Middle Way—these are the three contemplations of the cause. Regarding the initial phase of generating faith, which consists of the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha’s body of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana-kāya*): through the contemplation of the fruit, one attains the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and through the attainment of correspondence, one attains the causal form-body (*rūpakāya*).

By taking the causal retribution and Dharma-bodies as examples for the form-body, this constitutes the text on the partial realization of Buddhahood. This is divided into two parts: first, the extensive explanation of the First Abode (*prathamavihāra*); second, [the subsequent stages].
The explanation establishing the forty-two stages by way of analogy and illustration consists of two parts in the initial section: first, the explanation of one realm; second, the nine realms.
Regarding the first, it clarifies that at the moment of the initial arousal of the bodhicitta in the First Abode (Prathamacittotpāda-vihāra), one simultaneously attains the three bodies (*trikāya*).

By destroying ignorance and realizing the Middle Way, the three delusions are transformed, the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) increase in wisdom and virtue, and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) arises. Therefore, when one is aroused, all are aroused; when one produces [virtue], all virtues are produced.
The wisdom of all the *nirmāṇakāya*s is itself the objective realm of all the *saṃbhogakāya*s, which is itself the *dharmakāya*.
Without before or after, one realizes the three bodies and the three wisdoms with a single mind. Upon attaining the *saṃbhogakāya*, one attains the wondrous form of the Tathāgata;

upon reaching all *nirmāṇakāya*s, one opens the secret treasury; and upon reaching its center, one realizes the *dharmakāya*. The three bodies are thus differentiated, yet they are capable of giving rise to the Great [Vehicle].
Employing emanated bodies throughout a hundred worlds to manifest as Buddhas in response to the capacities of sentient beings, he manifests the wheel of the body through various physical forms;

he manifests the wheel of speech by reaching all sounds with a single voice to preach the Dharma; and he manifests the wheel of unwavering, equal, and pleasing intent by discerning the faculties of beings.
Regarding the accomplishment of the Eight Phases of Enlightenment: first, descending from Tuṣita Heaven; second, entering the womb; third, birth; fourth, renunciation; fifth, subduing [Māra]...
"If [the Buddha] accomplishes the Way at the sixth stage, turns the Wheel of Dharma at the seventh, and enters Nirvāṇa at the eighth, how much more so for the nine dharma-realms and the three wheels?

This passage uses the few to illustrate the many. Regarding the second dwelling, there are a thousand Buddhas in the world who manifest through transformation; from the third dwelling onwards, including those on the stages of practice, the stages leading toward enlightenment (*saṃmukhī-bhūmi*), and the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), they surpass the former immeasurably until reaching the ultimate Buddha.
This section is divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation of the meaning of "Buddha."

Next, regarding the phrase "The Buddha possesses immeasurable virtues," the following section points to the expanded initial text, which consists of three parts: the Dharma, the metaphor, and the application.

As for the term "one who speaks": it refers to one who proclaims through the wheel of the mouth, extols the four analytical knowledges from the tip of the tongue, and causes the eight qualities of voice to flow forth for the ears to perceive;
thus it is said, "one who names and speaks the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Alternatively, it refers to one who speaks the *sūtra*, *geya*, *itivṛttaka*, and *jātaka*.

It has also been said that among the twelve divisions of the scriptures—namely, *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, and *upadeśa*—the "small" category lacks the three [last] types while the "great" category contains all nine;
the "great" category lacks the three [first] types while the "small" category contains all nine. As for the eighty thousand treasuries of the Dharma, this is stated in the *Bhadrapāla-kalpika-sūtra*.
It is said that from the Buddha’s initial generation of the mind of awakening until the distribution of his relics, there were three hundred and fifty dharma-gates;

each gate contains the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), totaling two thousand one hundred perfections. By using these perfections to destroy the fourfold afflictions (*kleśa*), they combine to form eight thousand four hundred.
Calculating one perfection as equivalent to ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*), this results in eighty-four thousand dharma-gates. If one were to expand upon these eight...
The fourteen thousand treasuries of Dharma are designated by way of the Truth of Suffering; if designated by way of the Truth of Origination, they are the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction;
if designated by way of the Truth of the Path, they are the eighty-four thousand gates of *dhāraṇī*;

and if designated by way of the Truth of Cessation, they are the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*. Furthermore, the six perfections—namely, the six *pāramitās*—are also called the eighty-four [thousand].
The six perfections of the thousandfold limitlessness consist of four kinds, namely: arising and ceasing, non-arising, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned.

These are the four teaching gates. Regarding the "four *siddhāntas*," the term *siddhānta* means "pervasive," and *dāna* means "giving. Because all Buddhas employ these four dharmas to universally bestow [benefits] upon sentient beings, they are called the four *siddhāntas*.
When a hearer reaches the stage of receiving and practicing them, this corresponds to the world-level [truth] of faith and precepts.

Upon its opening and development, it is "human" (*pudgala*); upon the melting of the ice, it is "counteractive" (*pratipakṣa*); upon becoming flowing water, it is the "ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the world arising from the fruit, "joy" is the name for the human, "arising of good" is the designation for counteraction, and "extinguishing evil" is the ultimate meaning of entering into principle.
As for the three, two, or one: the three are the ultimate meanings; the two are the mundane.

Regarding the realms that benefit humans, there is first the realm of the world alone; if one attains the corresponding [realms], this refers to the practitioner who follows through faith (*śraddhānusārin*).

From the arising of understanding through the opening [of the Dharma], they listen to and study the sūtras and śāstras, inquire about their meaning, and practice from cause to fruit, thus delighting in silence.

This is the practitioner who follows the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), who sits upright in contemplation, fuses the mind with the *dharmadhātu*, and enters realization in accordance with the mind, attaining the fruit without deviation. This is precisely delusion.
The transformation of wisdom is clarity, not darkness; it is the realization of reality and the practice that does not align with the petty, external, or ordinary seekers.
To speak of them as having a single object of focus is for the sake of those who dwell in arising and ceasing.

To speak of all conditions and dharmas as arising and ceasing is precisely the twelve gates—non-arising, immeasurable, and unconditioned—encompassing the distinct and the perfect, wherein each gate brings benefit through the four *siddhāntas*.

Regarding the explanation of the contemplations (*guan*), there are two parts: first, the preliminary presentation listing the scriptures and indicating their locations; second, the current explanation of the intent, which concludes by establishing the relationship between body and wisdom.

This latter section also has two parts: first, the explanation of the sequence; second, the explanation of the single mind. The first part has three sections: first, explaining emptiness to establish the *saṃbhogakāya*;

second, explaining the provisional to establish the *nirmāṇakāya*; third, explaining the middle to establish the *dharmakāya*. "Knowing the illness and recognizing the medicine" refers to the application of the four [truths] and the fourfold analysis of contemplation.
The application of the Dharma-meaning of the Four Truths is threefold: first, discerning the contemplation of the four aspects of Suffering and Accumulation is called "knowing the illness";

second, discerning the contemplation of the four aspects of the Path and Cessation is called "identifying the medicine"; and third, employing the phrasing and eloquence to administer the medicine according to the illness so that it may be ingested and practiced is called "the function of entering into the conventional.
This is the utility of knowing the sequential Dharma-gate, which uses the four kinds of methods to examine the capacities of beings within the ten Dharma-realms.

Faults do not diminish; when the faculties are matured, one delivers others according to their capacities, and the realization of principle—whether great or small—is accomplished for both those within and outside the realms.

Through the *upāya-kauśalya* (skillful means), one illuminates and knows that emptiness comes first, the provisional follows, and the Middle Way is last; therefore, this is called "sequential," which is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-śāsana*).

Next, the text explaining the "One Mind and Three Contemplations" is divided into three parts: first, the explanation; second, citing the treatise as proof; third, the concluding praise. The first part is further divided into three, beginning with the demonstration.

First, the location and the explanation of the meaning; second, the sequential classification revealing the accomplishment of the three bodies and wisdom through the three contemplations; third, the citation of treatises from the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* to establish the proof;

fourth, the praise of the subtle and wondrous nature of these contemplations; and finally, the conclusion praising their perfect fusion and sovereign freedom as being neither identical nor different, thereby completing the summary of how these wondrous contemplations encompass all phenomena.

In the commentary on the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, there is first the formal explanation and second the conclusion. Regarding the latter, the integration of these three bodies has three parts: first, the Dharma; second, the metaphor; and third, the application of the analogy to the teaching.

Within the first part [the Dharma], there are again two sections: first, the translation of the names and a general explanation; second, the specific explanation beginning with "The Dharma-body. Within the first of these, there are again two sections: first, the translation of the names;

and second, the general explanation based on the Two Truths for the sake of sentient beings, beginning with "Furthermore, the Buddha originally has no body," which first follows the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha-satya*).

Following the worldly conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the specific explanation of the three bodies (*trikāya*) is divided into two parts: first, the explanation; second, the conclusion. The first part has three sections:

the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Regarding the Dharma-body, there are two sections: first, the explanation; second, the conclusion, which states: "This is precisely the body that is no-body.

The first section [of the Dharma-body] further has two parts: first, the explanation of the body, lifespan, and measure; second, the explanation of the measure. Regarding the Enjoyment-body, there are likewise three parts: the explanation of the body, lifespan, and measure. Second...

The body of the Śākya [Buddha] is further divided into three parts: first, citing two sūtras to demonstrate its characteristics; second, using the analogy of "as the object, so the wisdom" to show how they mutually constitute one another;

third, explaining that the Dharmakāya is not a [physical] body, concluding by establishing that the lifespan of the Dharma is neither [finite] life nor non-life, and explaining that its measure is neither measurable nor immeasurable.
Regarding the Nirmāṇakāya (Response Body), there are also three aspects: namely, that its body and lifespan can be known; that wisdom is merged with the essence; and next...
Regarding the meaning of the three bodies (*trikāya*): wisdom is the *saṃbhogakāya*, the body is the *dharmakāya*, and that which can give rise to great function is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
This is illustrated by the metaphor of mercury below; the section on the *dharmakāya* below correlates with the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and the eighty [years].

Both of these refer to the lifespan within the realm of traces: nineteen years until renouncing the world, thirty years until attaining enlightenment, and at age eighty, he proclaimed his entry into *nirvāṇa*.
Next, regarding these three bodies, the essence and qualities are fused and integrated.

In the explanation of the essence, there are two parts: first, a general explanation; second, a detailed analysis. The first [general explanation] consists of three sections: the Dharma, the metaphor, and the application of the Dharma.

This, in turn, has two parts: first, clarifying the primary essence; second, being adorned with the three qualities. Regarding the second [detailed analysis], it is divided into three: first, one should apply it according to conventional categories.

Regarding the body (*kāya*), first, in terms of the meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*), it corresponds to the *dharmakāya*; second, in terms of the meaning of "attainment," it corresponds to the *saṃbhogakāya*.

The commentary on the text is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the differing interpretations established by ancient masters; second, from "Now, as for... onwards, the actual explanation, which is further divided into three sections.

First, the headings are listed; second, the three points are explained; third, from "Furthermore, by means of cultivating the mind... onwards, the conclusion of the headings, which is itself divided into three parts. First, the establishment of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the school.
The meaning next clarifies that the primary tenet is the contemplation of the mind. Regarding the four types [of lands] below, the names of the lands are briefly listed;

because the purity of the mind is the cause and the purity of the Buddha-land is the fruit—since one attains birth in those lands by cultivating the sixteen contemplations with a pure mind—this is established as the tenet.

"Each has its own pure and impure" is the explanation below. Within this explanation, there are two parts: first, a brief summary; second, a detailed explanation beginning with "The evil [world of] Saha."

Regarding "ordinary beings and sages dwelling together," this refers to the ten dharma-realms (dharmadhātu) residing together; since the six paths of existence and the four classes of noble ones constitute these ten realms, they are called "dwelling together.

All four teachings have those who dwell together through birth: in the *Zang* (Tripitaka) Teaching, from the initial five methods of stopping the mind up to the stage of the Arhat’s approach, such persons are all born in this land;
in the *Tong* (Shared) Teaching, from the first bhūmi up to the sixth bhūmi; and in the *Bie* (Distinct) Teaching, from the ten stages of faith up to the sixth [stage].

The "Abiding in Rectifying the Mind" (Zhengxin-zhu) refers to those from the fifth stage downward up to the sixth level of faith and above, all of whom are born in the Land of Common Dwelling (Tongju-tu).

Regarding the defilement of this Land of Common Dwelling: within it, there are the six realms of existence which are defiled, and the four types of noble ones (*ārya*) which are pure. Within these four noble ones, there is further internal differentiation between the pure and the defiled.

Those who have realized the principle of the partial truth (*ekayāna*) are pure; however, because their ignorance (*avidyā*) has not yet been eliminated and they still possess residual traces, they are defiled. This analysis of the essence is subtle and skillful.

Regarding the distinction between the impure and the pure within the "coarse" [teachings]: analyzing the mind through the teachings of the *Tripiṭaka* (Āgama) is the "coarse"; cultivating the essence through the *Vaipulya* (Prajñāpāramitā) is the "skillful.

In both the *Vaipulya* and the *Sūtra* (Śrāvaka) teachings, one attains the fivefold Dharma-body; because one has destroyed view-delusions and afflictions, it is "pure," yet because one has not yet severed ignorance (*avidyā*), it is "impure.

The gradual approach corresponds to the *Pratyekabuddha* (Distinct Teaching), while the sudden entry corresponds to the *Bodhisattva* (Perfect Teaching). In both cases, realizing the principle is "pure," while the partial persistence of ignorance constitutes "impurity."

Regarding those in the Land of Expedient Means (upāya): in the Tripitaka Teaching, there are two types of persons, namely the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; in the Shared Teaching, there are four types of persons from the seventh stage up to the Buddha stage;
in the Distinct Teaching, there are thirty-four types of persons from the stage of non-retrogression within the ten faiths up to the tenth stage of dedication;
and in the Perfect Teaching, there are four types of persons—those from the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth faiths upward—all of whom are born into the Land of Expedient Means.

Regarding the delusions of the four stages of the Earth (bhūmi): taking the views (*dṛṣṭi*) of the three realms as the first stage; the thoughts (*vitarka*) of the desire realm as the second stage; the thoughts of the form realm as the third stage;

and the thoughts directed toward the formless realm as the fourth stage. If one calculates according to the external realms, the exhaustion of the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the three realms constitutes the fifth stage of delusion.
As for "attachment to form" and "attachment to the formless," the former two teachings exhaust both views and thoughts, thereby realizing the partial [truth].
In the latter two teachings of the True Dharma, one severs the delusions of views, thought, dust-and-sand, and ignorance, and realizes the principle of the Perfect Middle.

There is only a difference in the sequence and the single mind [of realization]. As for the Land of Real Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*): in the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings, there are no such persons;

in the Distinct Teaching, there are twelve types of persons, including those of the ten stages, Equal Enlightenment (*samayak-bodhi*), and Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), who sever ignorance and realize the Middle Way. In the Perfect Teaching, there are forty-one stages; as for the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*)...

When one attains equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), severing ignorance and realizing the Middle Way within the eternally quiescent *prabhāsvara*-land, this is the ultimate stage of wondrous enlightenment.

Here, the three virtues (*tri-dharma*) are perfected and the three bodies (*tri-kāya*) are fulfilled. The two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and severance (*prahāṇa*) are neither arising nor ceasing; this is called *nirvāṇa*.

It is the purely pure Buddha-land, the supreme grade of the *prabhāsvara*-land, wherein the Buddha alone dwells. Body and land are non-dual, both possessing the four virtues (*catuḥ-guṇa*). As for the intermediate [grade]...

In the lower two grades of the Land of Peaceful Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*), there is both purity and defilement. When one realizes the principle and wisdom becomes clear, delusions are exhausted and the principle is fully realized; thus, the wisdom of abandonment is complete.

Among the three grades of rebirth through the cultivation of the mind and wondrous contemplation—namely, the sixteen contemplations upon the primary and secondary fruits—one is able to be reborn in the Pure Land.
Each and every one of these is called "wondrous" because they all possess the three contemplations of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way. Such is their merit.

The "emptiness" contemplation (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) that severs [delusions] accomplishes the *saṃbhogakāya* by destroying the delusions of the four abodes; the "provisional" contemplation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) accomplishes the *nirmāṇakāya* by destroying the delusions of the sands of the Ganges;

and the "middle" contemplation (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*) accomplishes the *dharmakāya* by destroying the delusion of ignorance. Thus, the three contemplations are accomplished, the three virtues (*triguṇa*) are perfected as the fruit, and the three delusions are destroyed.
The three bodies are manifested: the cause is termed the three contemplations, and the fruit is termed the three virtues. In this way, cause and fruit are not [separate].

The second [aspect] is the sovereign interpenetration of the two: it is three within one, and one within three; it is neither three nor one, yet it is both three and one, with the wondrousness residing therein.
The verse says: In the contemplation of emptiness, the nature is ungraspable; In the contemplation of the provisional, phenomena accord with the Dharma-realm;
In the contemplation of the middle, the essence is equal and the principle is non-dual. It is three within one, yet the constant manifestation remains vividly present. Such are its virtues.
It is named "Wondrous Contemplation.

Within the categories of the teachings (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*), it is divided into four parts: first, clarifying the period of the teaching; second, clarifying the translation; third, clarifying its inclusion within the Piṭakas; and fourth, distinguishing it from others.

Regarding the first point, "the Mahāyāna Vaipulya teachings," this refers to the flavor of clarified butter (*ghṛta-rasa*) produced at the third period; it elucidates the "Full" (*pūrṇa*) in contrast to the "Half" (*ardha*).

The characteristics of these teachings are thereby clarified: although the characteristics of the five flavors of teaching were not the primary intent of the various sections [of the scriptures], they are understood incidentally as the general framework for the Buddha’s appearance in the world to bestow and open [the path].

Through the five flavors, the faculties of beings are harmonized, and the application and reduction of the teachings follow their respective capacities for realization and entry, such that each stage becomes clearly distinct (as stated at length).
Thus, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: "For example, from a cow comes milk; from milk comes curd; from curd comes [butter]."
From fresh butter (*sarpis*) comes matured butter (*navanīta*); from matured butter comes clarified butter (*ghṛta*). This is an analogy for the five flavors. It begins by saying:
"Just as from the Buddha emerge the twelve divisions of the scriptures; from the twelve divisions of the scriptures emerges the *Sūtra*;

The five periods of the Dharma in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* correspond to the first analogy: "From the cow comes milk. This refers to the flavor of milk, which corresponds to the *Avataṃsaka* (Huayan) Sudden Teaching.

The *Tetra-amṛta* (Four Flavors) corresponds to the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which constitute the fifth flavor. The *Wondrous Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*) alone reveals the Perfect Teaching by opening up the provisional;

and third, the arousal of the mind toward the Great Vehicle through cause and effect, which is unique to the Mahāyāna and involves the simultaneous transport of both self and others. The conclusion is as can be understood. Second, the Buddha told Vaidehī: "This..."
