and fourth, praising the appropriateness of the inquiry, wherein the resonance between the Way and its response perfectly accords with the principle of the capacity [of the listener], whereby one immediately attains the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

These sūtras are of three kinds, namely: the Dharma, the parable, and the application of the Dharma. Within the section on the Dharma, there are three parts: first, commanding Ānanda to expound extensively for the assembly; second, the Buddha’s own instruction; [and third, the conclusion].
Practicing the sublime contemplation, the three reveal the Buddha’s power, whereby one attains the vision of the Pure Land. Regarding "the Buddha’s power," there are three:
first, the power of Śākyamuni’s teaching; second, the power of Amitābha’s vows; and third, the power of the protection and mindfulness of all Buddhas of the ten directions.

In the analogy, the contemplation of the mind is like a mirror, the land manifested therein is like the face, and the transformation of the mind is like the reflected image. The passage beginning with "seeing that land" correlates this to the ultimate reality (*anupapatti*). It is non-arising.
Because the practitioner perceives this Pure Land as corresponding to their original seeking-mind, they give rise to the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) and immediately attain it at that moment.
Those who hear the teaching on the meaning of *Miaoguan* (Wondrous Contemplation) will only attain it later; thus, the Buddha employs skillful means to cause them to cultivate wondrous causes.

By practicing diligently according to the instructions, when the causes are perfected and the fruit is fulfilled, they attain the Patience of Non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and enter the first stage (*prathama-vihāra*).

"You are an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). The subsequent sutra passage has two parts: first, it rebukes the ordinary person for lacking power; second, it reveals that the noble ones (*ārya*) possess the necessary conditions.

The first part [shows] that the shadow-obstruction lacks noble virtue; the second part [shows] that the mental characteristics lack great superiority. "Seeing the object is not remote, as I do now," and so forth. The following inquiry has two parts:
first, how one attains vision through the causes of one's own practice; second, how one performs contemplation to give birth [to realization] for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
The Pure Land.

In the response, the sixteen contemplations answer the instruction to teach me right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). The text consists of three parts: the heading, the enumeration, and the judgment. Within the judgment, there are two sections;
first, the thirteen contemplations contemplate the place of rebirth, manifesting the excellence of the land and revealing its wondrousness, thereby causing one to contemplate the pure realm.
Beholding the Ultimate Sage and cultivating the practices of the supreme causes and wondrous deeds, one realizes the wondrous fruit within a single thought-moment.

Is this not entrusting oneself to the object to accomplish contemplation, transforming the defiled into the pure, destroying the three delusions, and manifesting the three bodies? When the causes of contemplation are perfected and the virtues of the fruit are fulfilled, the responses of sentient beings differ;
all attain rebirth after these three contemplations. As the text says: "The person who attains rebirth is like one pointing out a direction on a given day."
The merit of destroying darkness is like the Middle Way (Madhyamaka) view, which eliminates the delusion of ignorance to realize the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

The virtue of water in washing away and clarifying turbidity is like the Counterfeit View (*prajñapti-dṛṣṭi*), which severs the delusions of "dust-sand" [infinite afflictions] to realize the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Earth serves as the basis for the retributive environment, just as the Sitting View (*āsana-dṛṣṭi*) provides the seat upon which the body rests.
Space, like the Void View (*ākāśa-dṛṣṭi*), destroys the evil of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) to realize the Retribution-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). This sequence follows the order above.

When practicing the third [stage], one abides in a single mind. Why is this? It is because the provisional (*jia*) is identical to emptiness (*kong*), emptiness is identical to the middle (*zhong*), and the middle is identical to emptiness and the provisional.
These three contemplations (*sanguan*) are mutually fused, being neither one nor different; they are three while being one, and one while being three.

They are neither three nor one, yet they are three and one—perfectly integrated and sovereign. If such is the wondrous contemplation, how could it be the same as the "mere middle" (*danzhong*) or "single emptiness"?
Is it not the case that those who rely solely on solitary contemplation for liberation lack the threefold contemplation?

Regarding the first section, the "Contemplation of the Body," the text is divided into five parts: (1) exhortation to practice, (2) performing the contemplation, (3) citing the object of contemplation, (4) the actual instruction on observation, and (5) the conclusion.

In the initial text, there are two sections: first, clarifying the response of the Buddha; second, exhorting the practice of contemplation. As for the phrase "All things are not themselves... [the text continues].

Simplifying the essentials, all see the sun set; this constitutes the fourth stage of the contemplation within the four teachings. This section has two parts: first, the cultivation of the practice; second, the completion of the contemplation once the sun has set.
The initial text has two sections: first, the method; second, the analogy. Regarding sitting upright to distinguish it from walking, standing, and lying down:

walking involves excessive restlessness (*auddhatya*), while lying down leads to dullness (*styāna*). Standing for long periods causes fatigue; therefore, one is instructed to sit. One sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*), with the left leg [over the right].
Pressing the right foot with the left foot and the left foot with the right foot enables the body and mind to remain unmoving, sustained by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
One must focus intently on the sun with an undistracted mind, remaining fixed upon its specific characteristics. Regarding the interpretation of the scriptural analogy:
the setting sun represents the dharma that is illustrated, while the suspended drum illustrates the clarifying metaphor.
Within the second section on the contemplation of water, there are three parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent to clarify the object of contemplation;

second, the practice; and third, the conclusion. Within the sequential explanation of the cultivation of contemplation, there are four parts. The first three are as stated in the text. The fourth, the concluding passage, has four sections:

first, a general clarification of the inner and outer luminosity of the ground, the light of the various jewels beneath the earth, and the various marks of adornment upon the earth; next, the explanation of the adornments within the void.
The light and colors of the precious banners beneath the earth, and their metaphors (as detailed at length):

within each jewel, in the four voids below, there are colored lights of the sun, stars, moon, pavilions, flowers, banners, and musical instruments; a pure breeze proclaims the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding these eight kinds of pure breezes, as stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*: first, they are not cold; second, they are not hot; third, they are stirring and harmonious.
Fourth, harmony is incomparable; fifth, proceeding gradually without agitation; sixth, not being too slow; seventh, not being too fast;

eighth, attaining universal suitability and equilibrium through a mind that gathers all things. Regarding the three types of bonds, first the sequence of the bonds is established, followed by the clarification of the accomplishment of contemplation.

In the third stage, regarding the two benefits for those below that were announced by the Buddha, first is the proclamation of the benefit of the visualization, and second is the clarification of the benefits themselves.

Within the benefits, there are two parts: first, this world, and second, other worlds. When this visualization is perfected, grave offenses are extinguished and one will certainly be reborn in a pure land;
of this there is no doubt. Since the visualizations of the sun and water are situated in this world, they are employed as skillful means for the subsequent visualizations.
It cannot extinguish sins.
Regarding the "Adornment of the Two Luminosities Contemplated by the Four Trees," there are two parts: first, the adornment of the characteristics of the trees; second, the adornment within the void.

The first section of the sūtra has four points: namely, their height and breadth are complete, they are adorned with the seven treasures, they mutually adorn one another, and they are wondrously true.
A net of jewels covers it from above for one *yojana* (forty *li*), reaching a height of three million two hundred thousand *li*.

Next, in mid-air, there are two aspects: the Dharma and the simile. Within the Dharma aspect, there are four: the jeweled nets, the seven-jeweled flower palaces, five hundred billion celestial youths, and natural *maṇi* necklaces.
Third, regarding the arising of the Dharma, there are two: the Dharma and the simile, which correspond to each other.

The four middle [points] refer to the arrangement of the leaves, their succession, and the fullness of the flowers and fruits; as for the size of the leaves and the color and appearance of the flower petals—these are the fifth.

Regarding the contemplation of the five ponds, there are five points as in the text. Within the substance of the ponds, there are three: first, the summary of what precedes and the generation of what follows;

second, the enumeration of the three substances; third, the characteristics of the pond itself. Below these are four points: first, the water itself and its branches; second, the channels and the sand at the bottom of the pond; third, the number and quantity of the pond flowers. Third.

The *Ming suixin* (Clarifying the Mind According to Its Contents) contains two sets of Four Noble Truths that encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the Six Pāramitās and the four types of practitioners. These are:

the Truths of Arising and Ceasing (*utpādanirodha*), Non-arising (*anutpāda*), the Immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the Unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*). In the first two, one eliminates the afflictions of views and mental defilements (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the realm of desire and form, attaining the five factors of the Dharma-body (*pañcadharmaskandha*).

In the latter two, one eliminates the affliction of ignorance (*avidyā*) beyond those realms, entering [the path] either gradually or instantaneously to equally realize the three bodies (*trikāya*). This sūtra belongs to the Vaipulya (Extensive) division.

Therefore, among the benefits for the four types of persons who cultivate the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there is the sound of the jewel-bird (*ratna-pakṣin*), which is soft and constantly praises the Triple Gem.

In the sixth contemplation, there are five parts: first, a general summary; second, a detailed analysis; third, within the detailed analysis, first contemplating the pavilions, then contemplating the towers and the music in the air;

fourth, concluding the characteristics of the contemplation; fifth, revealing the benefits and distinguishing the correct from the erroneous aspects of the contemplation; and finally, contemplating the trees and the void.
There were celestial musicians in the air, and their exquisite banners all praised the Triple Gem.
In the seventh contemplation, he was commanded to listen and permitted to speak; with sincere attention, he heard the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

Next, he was permitted to speak on the three exhortations to uphold [the teachings] and the extensive explanation of the two Buddhas manifesting their physical forms. Within this, first the manifestation of the teacher and disciple is clarified, followed by the clarification of...
Within the light, first the Dharma and then the metaphorical forms and characteristics cannot be apprehended; comparing these three as the future, the request consists of two parts:

first, prostrating by touching the feet to express reverence; second, formally declaring the actual request. Within the request, there are two parts: first, clarifying that one’s own self was able to see [the Buddhas] due to the Buddha;
second, on behalf of future sentient beings, asking how one should practice contemplation to behold the Three Holy Ones, and entreating the Buddha’s compassionate grace.
Not departing from his original vow, he extensively proclaimed and expounded the teachings, opening the gate of ambrosia to universally benefit the great assembly.

By teaching both the doctrine and contemplation regarding the primary and secondary aspects [of reality], he enabled them to attain the fruits of sainthood; thus benefiting both self and others, he finally fulfilled his original intention. With feet pressed together in earnest devotion, his purpose lay herein.

The Buddha, out of great compassion, expounded the teachings on the body, the seat, and the attendants in accordance with the request; these were clearly and distinctly revealed, appearing as if present before one's eyes.
All shall achieve the rebirth of the three grades and ascend together to the Pure Land. First, the Method for Accomplishing the Seat: there are five parts. 1.
Contemplate the precious ground and the petals of the lotus. Next, descend from Śākyamuni’s Vaiḍūrya [Vajra] to contemplate the jewel within the lotus pedestal.
3. From above and below that pedestal, contemplate the precious banners of the lotus. 4. From above and below the banners, contemplate the precious canopies of the lotus. 5. From...
There are five hundred *koṭis* of precious jewels; looking down at the luster and colors of these jewels, the initial passage has two parts: first, a general description, and second, a detailed one.

Within the detailed section there are six points—namely, the color of the petals, the light of the veins, the size of the flowers, the number of petals, the jewels, and the mutual manifestation of their pervasive coverage over the ground.

Regarding the flower pedestals, there are two points: first, clarifying the substance of the pedestal, and second, clarifying its adornments. As stated in the *Ratnolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*: "Vai... [The text continues with the Sanskrit term *vaiḍūrya*].

The *Laṅkāvatāra* jewel is of pure, genuine golden color and resides in the Brahma palace. When Bodhisattvas are born there, they draw upon the power of their own roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), whereby this jewel spontaneously appears within a casket.
It is capable of subduing Māras, neutralizing poisons, and so forth, as explained at length in the Sūtra.

Regarding the second section, "Benefiting Beings According to Their Capacities," there are three parts: first, the general; next, the specific; third, the contemplation of Buddha-activities; and fifth, the elucidation of future benefits.

In the middle three [sections], first the Dharma, then the analogy, and third the clarification of the benefits. Within the clarification of the benefits, there are two parts: first the general, then the specific.

In the eighth [section], the contemplation of the one, there are two parts: first the summary and then the explanation. Within the explanation, the sutra has two parts: first the explanation and then the summary, beginning with "This is for...

In the sequential explanation of the contemplation, regarding the first, the bodies of all Buddhas, there are three parts: first the inquiry, then the explanation, and third the exhortation to practice the cause.
Since the fruit serves as the verification, one should therefore single-mindedly look downward. Regarding that Amitābha, there are two stages: first, contemplating the True Body (*dharmakāya*);
second, visualizing that Buddha. Looking downward involves two parts: first, practicing the visualization; second, the completion of the visualization.

The practice of visualization consists of two: first, the Buddha; second, the Bodhisattvas. Within the Buddha, there are three: first, the Buddha-body; second, the supporting land; third, seeing these matters as they are. This concludes the section.

Regarding the analogy for the *dharmāyatana* (the sense-base of mental objects): after having seen this matter, one next contemplates the Bodhisattva as twofold—first, one contemplates the seat, and second, one contemplates the image [of the Buddha].
When this contemplation is accomplished, there are three subsequent stages of clear visualization: first, seeing the holy body and the seat through light;
second, hearing the sublime Dharma; and third, regarding the Dharma heard upon entering and emerging from meditative absorption, one abandons the heterodox and follows the orthodox.

The Ninth Contemplation: Observing the Size of the Buddha’s Body. This sutra has two parts: first, observing Amitābha; second, for those who have witnessed this matter, observing the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Regarding Amitābha, there are further two sections: first, individual observation; second, a general summary. Within the individual observation, there are six points:

(1) clarifying the color and size of the body; (2) clarifying the ūrṇā-kośa and the eyes; (3) clarifying the extent of the bodily radiance; (4) the emanated Buddhas and attendants; (5) clarifying... [text fragment].
The Buddha’s marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) and the sixfold luminous light universally encompass them; regarding these marks and signs of light, the following section provides a general summary.

Regarding the relinquishing of the body in other worlds, the following four sections raise the benefits and exhort practice. The sūtra contains five parts: first, clarifying the benefits; second, "Therefore, the wise person" and below, the formal exhortation;
third, the exhortation to contemplate the ūrṇā-kośa (white tuft); fourth, "Seeing the immeasurable" and below, seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions; fifth, attaining the vision of all [Buddhas].
The Buddha descends to bestow the prophecy.

In the tenth contemplation, the first is the contemplation of the marks of the body, which has four parts: first, contemplating the marks of the body with light rays flowing forth in myriads; second, contemplating the color of the arms and the *śrīkhaṇḍa* necklaces;

third, universally contemplating the color and light of the palms and fingers as they shine everywhere; fourth, contemplating the wheels on the soles of the feet and the lotus pedestals spreading throughout.
In the first section, "The Fullness of the Initial Body," there are six parts: (1) clarifying the dimensions, color, and form of the body; (2) clarifying the light of the uṣṇīṣa;

(3) clarifying the marks of the emanation-buddhas' bodily radiance; (4) clarifying the dimensions of the buddhas on the celestial crown; (5) clarifying the facial complexion and the jewel between the eyebrows; and (6) clarifying that the light-buddhas attend [the main figure] in infinite numbers.

In the second section, "Similarities and Differences Between [the Bodhisattva] and the Buddha," there are three parts: (1) first, the similarities; (2) next, the differences; and (3) the conclusion regarding the sequence of compassion and flowers.
The Sūtra states: "When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara attains Buddhahood, he shall be named Tathāgata King of the Mountain of All Radiant Merits;
his world shall be renamed 'Possessing All Precious Jewels,' and it shall surpass the Land of Ultimate Bliss in every respect."

The eleventh contemplation, within the section on the spiritual power of the light of the primary cause, has three parts: first, clarifying the extent of the body’s radiance; second, clarifying the characteristics of the body’s color and pores;
third, clarifying that wisdom can destroy hindrances. Within the second part, which is shared with Avalokiteśvara, there are two sections: first, clarifying the identity of the forms;

second, clarifying the correct visualization. The first of these has three sub-sections: first, clarifying how the bodily forms universally manifest as Buddhas; second, clarifying the spheres of activity.
The Ritual for Seated Meditation Adorned with Jewel Flowers and the Assemblage of Emanations for Preaching the Dharma to Deliver Sentient Beings.

In the beginning, there are three distinct features—the celestial crown, the topknot, and the jewel vase—while the remaining characteristics are identical [to those of Avalokiteśvara]. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"Bodhisattva Śrīmaṇi, in the World of Peace and Bliss, shall attain perfect enlightenment after Avalokiteśvara, becoming the Tathāgata named Well-Abiding Jewel King."

Regarding the three types of bonds (*saṃyojana*), there are four: first, the contemplation of the initial bond; second, the clarification of its benefits; third, the joint contemplation of both the noble ones and the two [types of] bonds;

and fourth, the contemplation of the deviant and the correct within the twelfth section on universal contemplation. The commentary text for this section is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the similarities and differences; second, providing an exegesis based on the text. First...

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the question; second, the answer, which begins with a general observation and proceeds to explain the visualization of the body. Within this section on visualizing the body, there are three parts:

first, the heading; second, the actual visualization of rebirth; third, the conclusion of the sequence of visualization. Regarding the four stages of rebirth: first, the act of rebirth; second, seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma; third, retaining it in memory without forgetting;
fourth, concluding that the visualization has been perfected by beholding both the primary and secondary environments (*āśraya* and *parivāra*). In the first of these, there are three sections.
First, visualize the body seated upon its throne, followed by the opening and closing of the lotus flower, and the three-colored light illuminating the body and eyes;

this is the thirteenth visualization. Within the second section on the manifestations of Amitābha, there are two parts: first, visualizing the Buddha, and second, visualizing the Bodhisattvas. Regarding the first [visualizing the Buddha], there are three sub-sections:
first, clarifying that the body’s dimensions are boundless and beyond the reach of ordinary beings; second, concluding with the Tathāgata’s vow-power; and third, [the subsequent sections].

The contemplation on the benefits achieved by the three Amitābha Buddhas below [the previous section] involves the Buddhas manifesting their bodies both collectively and individually according to the capacities of sentient beings;
next, from "Avalokiteśvara" onwards, one contemplates the two Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the fourteenth contemplation, the commentary (*shūmon*) is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the purpose of its inclusion; second, explaining the sutras and treatises in accordance with the text.

Regarding the three layers of questions and answers within the middle section—the first concerning the two vehicles, the second concerning women, and the third concerning those who commit the five heinous crimes and slander the Dharma—this is explained according to the text.
First, as for the intent of this introduction: it is because one contemplates both the primary and secondary fruits [of Buddhahood].

Specifically, by contemplating the wondrous land and the assembly of sages, one practices and accomplishes superior conduct in accordance with the teachings; thus, the perfect cause leads to the attainment of the fruit, wherein rebirth in the nine grades is assuredly true and authentic.

The general purport of this text is as follows: Vaidehī requests on behalf of herself and others for the sake of future generations regarding the practice of visualization; the Buddha responds with the appropriate teaching;

and he exhorts sentient beings according to the sharpness or dullness of their faculties through the three grades of rebirth. In the exegesis based on the text, there are two parts: first, a judgment on the differences in rank and vehicle among the three grades;

second, an explanation of the meaning according to the scripture. Regarding the section on the "Highest Birth in the Highest Grade," it is divided into two parts, the first of which provides a specific explanation.

The third section provides a concluding summary of the first part, which clarifies the cultivation of causes. This consists of two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. Within the explanation, there are two sections: first, the three minds; second, the three practices.

Each of these two groups contains four elements—namely, the heading, the inquiry, the arising, and the explanation followed by the conclusion. Regarding the time of rebirth in that land, the subsequent two sections clarify the meeting with conditions, which comprise five points:
first, meeting the assembly of sages; second, holding the precious platform; third, the Buddha emitting light; fourth, the arrival of Superb Friends to welcome one.

Receiving the five praises, his mind is exhorted so that his practice may achieve fulfillment. There are three [sections] regarding the attainment of rebirth therein: first, clarifying the joy of the three karmas;

second, seeing one’s own body riding upon a platform; third, being reborn at the appropriate time. Regarding the benefit after rebirth, there are three [sections]: first, that land; second, the ten directions;
third, one’s own country. In the first text, there are three [parts]: first, seeing the marks and features of the holy body; second, hearing...

Having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* three times, they subsequently realized the fruit [of enlightenment]. Regarding the two points concerning the ten directions—first, serving the various Buddhas;

second, receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)—the term "in a moment" (*muhūrta*) is defined according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* as follows: one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*;
sixty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*; thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*; and thirty *muhūrtas* [constitute one day and night].
One *muhūrta* constitutes a day and night; this is called a *muhūrta*, which means "a brief moment," like a person walking five *li*.
Regarding the second [grade] of those born from the superior class, there are five conditions encountered: first, the season; second, encountering the assembly of sages;

third, holding the precious platform; fourth, being welcomed; and fifth, receiving the prediction of enlightenment. Third, regarding the manner of birth, there are three stages: first, seeing one's own body ascend the platform; next...
1. Joining palms to praise the Buddha; 2. Swift rebirth [in the Pure Land]; 3. Going forth to benefit others; 4. The Sūtra on the Four Matters.
Regarding the first [rebirth], there are four parts: 1. The blossoming of flowers and the color of the body; 2. The holy assembly emitting light; 3. Hearing the Dharma due to past habitual practice;
4. Prostrating in worship; 5. Non-retrogression. This concludes the section on the lower birth of the superior grade.

The second, the *Zhíyuán jīng* (Sūtra on Encountering Conditions), has five points: first, the time; second, encountering the holy assembly; third, holding a flower; fourth, the transformation Buddha extending his hand;
fifth, praising the practitioner. Third, regarding the attainment of birth, there are two parts: first, seeing one’s own body ascend the seat; second, attaining rebirth.
According to the *Shíyí lùn* (Treatise on the Ten Doubts), the stage of non-retrogression has five aspects: first, the great compassionate power of the vows of Amitābha Buddha.
Therefore, one attains non-retrogression for two reasons: first, because the Buddha’s light constantly illuminates them and their bodhicitta constantly increases, they do not retrogress;

second, because the waterfowl, trees, forests, and the sounds of the wind and music all proclaim suffering, emptiness, and impermanence, those who hear them constantly give rise to thoughts of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and thus do not retrogress;
third, because that land is named the Land of Non-Retrogression, and the Buddhas’ bodhi—

First, because he has the Bodhisattva as a virtuous friend and lacks external malevolent conditions or demons, and internally lacks the three poisons which ultimately do not arise, he does not regress.
Second, after being born in that land for five lifetimes, his lifespan becomes immeasurable and equal to that of the Buddha; therefore, he does not regress.
Third, after four subsequent lifetimes, his benefit is such that he attains the "Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas"; therein, "illumination" refers to form-dharmas and mind.

The mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), the factors dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*), and the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) together constitute one hundred dharmas.

At the time of entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), these are all realized instantaneously and simultaneously. According to the Tiantai commentaries, the mental concomitants (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*) common to all stages (*mahābhūmika*) of all sentient beings consist of ten factors:

sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), desire (*chanda*), wisdom (*prajñā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), liberation (*adhimokṣa*), concentration (*samādhi*), and attention (*manaskāra*). The mind-king (*citta-rāja*) itself is the true cause of Buddha-nature (*tathāgata-garbha*).

The conceptualization (*saṃjñā*)-count and the wisdom (*prajñā*)-count are the *pariniṣpanna-hetu* (perfected cause) Buddha-nature; the remaining counts are the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditional cause) Buddha-nature.

When one count arises, the other nine aspects arise simultaneously, thus constituting a hundred counts. Although these hundred counts possess the three Buddha-natures, they are specifically termed the "three causal Buddha-natures" as they exist within the minds of sentient beings.

These hundred counts, when entering the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), likewise possess the three Buddha-natures; however, from the perspective of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), they are distinguished.
This is called the Buddha-nature as the condition-cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

This [realization] of the hundred entries and ten abodes, wherein the three Buddha-natures are perfectly realized, is also called the "Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas" (*śata-dharma-vibhāsa-mukha*), and is also called the "Three Virtues" (*tri-guṇa*) and the "Three Bodies" (*tri-kāya*), and so forth. The Sūtra has three sections: first, that land; second, the ten directions;

third, the time of entry into the stages. Regarding the first section, there are three parts: first, the blossoming of the flowers; second, clearly seeing the Buddhas; third, hearing the Dharma. That land...

The opening of the flowers distinguishes day from night; one day and one night [in the Sahā world] corresponds to one kalpa in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which constitutes one day and one night in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Fifteenth: The Superior Birth of the Middle Grade. Part Two: Encountering Conditions. Sub-section One: Encountering the Holy Multitude. Next, the Emission of Light...

[The section on] "Light" has three parts: (1) hearing the Dharma and attaining joy; (2) attaining rebirth therein; (3) seeing one's body seated upon a lotus pedestal. Next is the application of prostration.
[The section on] "Attaining Rebirth" has four parts. Within the subsequent "Benefits," there are three parts: (1) the lotus opening and hearing the Dharma;

(2) attaining the fruit; (3) being endowed with the Dharma. Regarding the Four Truths, the text is divided into five sections: (1) the Four Truths; (2) the Arhat; (3) attaining the Three Insights. Regarding the Three Insights: first, the transcendence... [text ends].

The knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*) in the present, and the knowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-jñāna*) in the future constitute the four [knowledges] and six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Regarding the five explanations of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the third consists of the heading, the explanation, and the judgment. Within the judgment, first the fruit, then the cause, and then the citation of the *Śāstra* to clarify that the four fruits are non-arising;
this is the reconciliation of the meanings of the Sūtras and Śāstras. Among those born in the intermediate state, the second encounters [the Buddha].
Regarding the three aspects within the conditions for rebirth: first, encountering the assembly of sages; second, the emission of light; and third, praise and welcome.
Regarding the three aspects of benefits after birth: first, the blossoming of flowers; second, praising the Buddha and hearing the Dharma; and third, attaining the fruit.

Regarding the third [section] on the middle grade of rebirth, there are three parts: namely, the teaching, the metaphor, and the application. Regarding the four aspects of benefits after birth: first, seeing the sages; second, ... [text ends].
Hearing the Dharma and attaining the three fruits—this is the sixteenth [section].
Regarding the "Superior Birth of the Lower Grade," the first part clarifies the causes, which is divided into two:

first, describing the commission of minor transgressions without grave accumulation; second, from "at the time when life is about to end" onwards, describing the cultivation of merit. Within the description of merit, there are two parts, the first being hearing the Dharma.
First, further eliminating the causes of evil by following the wise and below recollecting the Buddha; second, further eliminating the effects of evil.

Third, clarifying the conditions, which has two parts: first, the invitation of the assembly of sages; second, their praise and reception. Fourth, attaining birth, which has two parts: first, seeing the light of the Buddha; second, riding upon flowers to attain birth.

Fifth, the benefits after birth, which has five parts: first, the blossoming of the flower; second, the invitation of the sages; third, hearing [the Dharma]; fourth, [attaining] realization; fifth, [attaining] liberation.
The Dharma consists of four stages of generating the mind and five attainments of the fruit. Within the middle grade of the inferior [category], the first clarifies the causes, which are twofold:

first, the primary cause of evil; second, the causal factors for the fruit. Regarding the latter, there are three: first, violating the precepts; second, stealing the property of the Sangha; third, preaching the Dharma with impurity.
As for preaching the Dharma with impurity, there are four faults: first, preaching the Dharma with a light heart, not seeking one's own benefit; second, seeking fame; [and so forth].
1. Acting for one’s own benefit rather than transforming others; 2. harboring a competitive mind regarding the three lives; 3. seeking followers; 4. seeking worldly rewards; and 5.

concealing the correct teaching while preaching what is false—teaching the Dharma in such a manner is called "impure. Next, from "such a sinner" downward, [the text describes] the inferior fruits [of such actions].

From "meeting a virtuous friend" downward, the second section describes the virtues. Within the description of virtues, there are two parts: first, the description of the Buddha’s ten powers; second, the fivefold [perfections].
Having heard the two [aspects of] the Dharma-body, one obtains benefit; the sins of birth and death are removed, and the cool breeze appears.
Regarding the four benefits after the four types of birth, the first [section on] the lower grade of the lower birth first clarifies the cultivation of causes.

This section has two parts: first, marking the evil; second, obstructing the good. The first [of these] is further divided into two: first, the evil causes, as follows: [The text continues with the specific details of the evil causes.]
This foolish person next receives inferior and evil fruits; next, there is the obstruction of the good [within the five stages], where first the timing is clarified;

next, meeting a virtuous friend, where the teaching of the good friend is to bring mindfulness to three; that person’s suffering, where being oppressed by suffering prevents the arising of goodness four;

the teaching according to the ten recitations; and the benefit of the five recitations which eliminates transgressions. Within the recitation following the sound, one must possess four conditions: first, mindfulness of that Buddha.

Because one who possesses a vow will certainly be reborn, there must be four conditions: first, one must recite the name; second, one must do so with a sincere and virtuous mind, for if the mind is distracted, right mindfulness will not be established;
third, one must ensure that the sound does not cease until one enters into right contemplation; fourth, one must fulfill ten recitations to achieve swift accomplishment.
When these four conditions are complete, there is no further doubt, as explained in the *Ten Doubts* (Shi yi): "It is like a rope of ten bundles [of hemp]... [which can bind a thousand...].

Now, if a youth who has not yet mastered his skill can brandish a sword in a mere moment for several *kṣaṇas*, and if a stack of firewood accumulated over a thousand years is consumed in a short time by a fire lit with a single bean-sized spark—how much more so for one who, at the moment of death, possesses a fierce and sharp intention that is true and uninterrupted, thereby attaining birth in the Pure Land? In a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), one immediately attains rebirth. Fourth, regarding the benefits obtained, the scriptural text contains four points: 1. [First benefit] 2. [Second benefit] 3. [Third benefit] 4. [Fourth benefit] [The first point:

Just as a person who has committed the five grave offenses (*ānantarya*) or the ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala-karma*) is able to attain birth in the Pure Land through the power of the Buddha’s name, how much more so for those who have cultivated roots of goodness throughout their lives! Furthermore, even if one has committed various transgressions, if they encounter a virtuous friend who teaches them the profound Dharma, they will be able to repent and reform. If they recite the Buddha’s name with a sincere mind, they will surely attain birth. This is because the power of the Buddha’s name is inconceivable and surpasses all other powers. It is like a great fire that cannot be extinguished by water; likewise, the power of the Buddha’s name cannot be obstructed by any karmic hindrances. Therefore, one should know that the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name is supreme and unsurpassed. As the sutra says: "If a person hears the name of Amitābha Buddha and gives rise to a single thought of joy, they shall, at the end of life, be born in his land. This is the first benefit. [The second point: Moreover, if one recites the Buddha’s name with a focused mind, they will immediately see the Buddha’s physical form and hear his voice. The Buddha will extend his hand to welcome them, and they will be born in the Lotus Treasury World. Once born there, they will dwell in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). This is the second benefit. [The third point:

Furthermore, those who recite the Buddha’s name will be protected by the Buddhas of the ten directions. They will never again fall into the three evil realms (*tridurgati*). Even if they are currently suffering in the hells, they will be released upon hearing the Buddha’s name and will be reborn in the heavens. This is the third benefit. [The fourth point: Finally, those who recite the Buddha’s name will attain mastery over their lifespan. They will be able to manifest their bodies in various lands to teach and transform sentient beings according to their needs. This is the fourth benefit. Thus, the merits of reciting the Buddha’s name are immeasurable and boundless. One should diligently practice it without negligence.]
First, the flowers bloom; second, the two [types of beings] move the sages; third, they hear the Dharma and their offenses are extinguished; fourth, they resolve for Bodhicitta.

In the second major section on benefits, the first part clarifies the realization of the Path and the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpāda*). This section contains two points: first, it concludes the previous section and introduces the subsequent one;

within the introduction, there are three parts: first, beholding the environment and its inhabitants (the *dharmakāya* and *rūpakāya*); second, the three karmas receive and understand [the teaching]; third, the realization of the Path and the non-arising of dharmas.

Regarding the first contemplation on the two fruits—the environment and its inhabitants—based on the preceding scriptural passages, we see that after witnessing the Buddha’s lamentation, [Vimalakīrti] requested the place of rebirth and the causes for being born there.
The sutra states: "I only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively explain for me the place free from sorrow and affliction;
I shall be reborn there. It further says: "I only pray that the Buddha-Sun will teach me to contemplate the locus of pure karma. Thus, one should observe his request.
In her mind, Vaidehī lamented with grief, her thoughts encompassing both herself and others: first, she lamented her own past transgressions that resulted in the birth of this wicked son;

second, she lamented how Devadatta incited the King through delusion, causing him to kill his father and harm his mother, thereby bringing upon her such sorrow and affliction that her body and mind were withered and exhausted.

As the eight sufferings converged and she was confined within the deep palace, her connection to the cycle of birth and death was forever severed; thus, she requested the Pure Land, including both its environment and its inhabitants.

He replied to me: "You shall be reborn there. In accordance with the opportune conditions and at my request, he spoke; emitting light and smiling, he manifested himself throughout all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
Although Vaidehī saw that these lands were magnificent, radiant, and worthy of contemplation, she returned her devotion to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (An-yang).
Therefore, she requested again, saying: "All these Buddha-lands possess radiance, but I now wish to be born in [Sukhavatī]."
I pray that the World-Honored One will teach me how to contemplate and teach me right concentration (*samādhi*). I request instruction on contemplation and instruction on right concentration;
I request the visualization of the Buddha so that you may extensively explain the three types of pure karma and the sixteen sublime contemplations.

By diligently practicing according to these teachings, the cause will be perfected and the fruit fulfilled, and one will be reborn in the three grades of birth without any doubt. Thus, with the eye of the mind, one will see clearly and distinctly.

The Sūtra says: "Hearing what the Buddha has taught, up to the marks of being broad and long"—this refers to the first six contemplations, which are the pure fruits of the secondary environment (*upādāya-vipāka*).

"Seeing the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas" and below refers to the middle seven contemplations, which are the primary fruits (*mukhya-phala*). Next, the joyful heart that exclaims, "How unprecedented! constitutes the subsequent three contemplations.
These involve receiving understanding through the three karmas; this is the cultivation of causes and encountering conditions to obtain benefits, proceeding according to one's karma.
Because [the mind] arises, the mind gives rise to joy; because it abandons the defiled and returns to the pure, it exclaims that this is unprecedented.

Thus ends the Sixteen Contemplations. Third, one awakens to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Because one requests [the teaching], the mutual resonance of the Way is explained; through vast and great awakening, one attains the principle of the patience of non-arising.
As for "vast and empty" (*kōran*), the phenomena transform into the state of Great Awakening, and as the contemplation develops into vast emptiness, it becomes the realm of Great Awakening.
Severing evil and diminishing [afflictions] results in a vast, open wisdom; increasing merit and virtue leads to great awakening and the arising of the *dharmakāya*.

Attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) constitutes the two patiences of non-arising and quiescent extinction. Second, the clarification of the maidens' generation of the mind has two parts: first, the maidens themselves; second, the praise of the various goddesses.
Within the section on the maidens, there are four parts: first, the generation of the mind; second, the vow for rebirth; third, the Buddha’s prediction; and fourth, the attainment of *samādhi*.

In the introductory section of the circulation [of this text], the question regarding the meaning of the sutra is first posed, and the Buddha’s response contains three parts. First, the title of this sutra is "The Land of Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī-vyūha).
This refers to the initial six contemplations: contemplating the sun to indicate its location and dispel darkness; removing obscurity; water that can clarify and wash away all defilements;
ground as pure as lapis lazuli, transparent both inside and out; jeweled trees and jeweled pavilions; flowers, fruits, and bathing pools; and rivers flowing with the eight virtues. Fourth.
Subtly eliminating afflictions, they are summarized as one; when all visualizations are clear, this is the fruit of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment).
Below this is the fruit of the *upapatti-vipāka* (the body), consisting of the seven meditations on Amitāyus Buddha. These involve clearly visualizing the Buddha’s body, his seat, and his attendants.

Furthermore, there are the various meditations according to the capacities of practitioners, whether for oneself or others, which are also called "Purifying. Below this are the final three meditations, wherein the cultivation of the three karmas results in the nine grades of rebirth.
Regarding the attainment of rebirth and the response of the holy ones: because those of both sharp and dull faculties all proceed to the platform, it is said that they are born before all Buddhas.

Next, the benefits are explained in five parts: first, seeing the assembly of holy ones; second, being encouraged to hear the name and thereby obtain benefit; third, establishing the body through analogy; fourth, encountering superior friends;
and fifth, sitting at the site of enlightenment. As for the *puṇḍarīka* flower, this is translated as the white lotus; it is the most excellent and wondrous among all flowers.

Form (*rūpa*) is the root among all manifested colors and is the most weighty in the world; because sentient beings who mindfully recite the Buddha's name are honored by the world, this is cited as a metaphor to establish their supreme body.
Following this, the various perfections (*pāramitā*) and myriad practices constitute the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

They treat the chaff of ignorance to reveal the rice-grains of the true mark (*dharmatā*). By destroying the three delusions, the three virtues (*triguṇa*) are perfected, resulting in the fulfillment of the True, Responsive, and Transformational bodies to save sentient beings; thus, the great assembly is exhorted.
Diligently practicing and truly explaining the meaning of birth in the Pure Land as the essence and function of the Way:
those born into the family of all Buddhas do so because (1) the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*) is the family of all Buddhas, serving as the basis for the primary retribution of wisdom;

(2) the Treasury of Principle (*tattvagarbha*) is the family of all Buddhas, serving as that which is practiced by the Treasury of Practice (*caryāgarbha*); and (3) the Nature of the Objective Realm (*viṣayadharmatā*) is the family of all Buddhas, serving as the object of the three contemplations.
By observation, the four pure lands—compassion being the family of all Buddhas and the place to which all sentient beings return—are thus established.

The Land of Tranquil Light (*jigō*) is the fundamental realm, most expansive; the first, middle, and last three are its manifestations (*shaku*), gradually narrowing according to the capacities of beings.

Since these four dharmas exist within each of the three lands, yet differ according to the capacities of beings, it is said that the three lands—the Real Reward (*jissō-hōō*), Expedient Means (*hōben*), and Common Residence (*dōgyō*)—are employed through the teachings for the multitudes.

Regarding "Birth": when the Buddha returned through the air, he did so to increase the veneration of sentient beings. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "At that time, having been confined in prison, Vaidehī was distressed and emaciated;
she bowed toward Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in homage to the Buddha. Having spoken these words, she wept with tears falling like rain as she bowed from afar to the Buddha.
This is what it means to increase the veneration of sentient beings. As for "following his words," the Sūtra says: "And so she acted accordingly."
"This means that in the past, the World-Honored One constantly sent Maudgalyāyana and Ānanda to come and comfort me;
now that I am filled with sorrow and distress, I even pray that he would send Ānanda to meet me.

In accordance with her words, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of Vaidehī while on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, commanded his two disciples to come through the air; the Buddha then vanished from that place.

Emerging from the royal palace with a golden body, seated upon a precious lotus flower, and attended on both sides by celestial beings making offerings, Vaidehī threw herself to the ground and wept piteously, lamenting that her beloved son had been treacherously and unjustly murdered.

She requested birth in the Pure Land out of weariness with this defiled realm. The Buddha, moved by compassion, extensively expounded the Dharma for her; she practiced according to these instructions, and because of this cause, [she attained rebirth].
Because the perfect fruit and the full capacity of the sentient beings are in harmonious correspondence, they are able to be born in the Pure Land through supernatural powers;

thus, for the benefit of sentient beings, once their capacities have been benefited, one proceeds by means of spiritual transformations. The fundamental substance of the Dharmakāya pervades the entire Dharma-realm without distinction of self and other, and there is neither going nor coming.

Nevertheless, in order to accord with the capacities of beings, it manifests these transformed appearances. Furthermore, this is a brief record based on my own mirror-like reflection upon the deluded sentiments of former masters.

How could later worthies dare to transmit another version? However, Fǎcōng’s learning was meager and his wisdom shallow; he had not yet exhausted the Three Piṭakas, his virtue was thin and his status low, and his talent did not exceed the ordinary track.

Moreover, since the traces of the Buddha-dharma are profound and mysterious, how could the intelligence of an ordinary person like me suffice to propagate them? Relying on the original text, I have roughly divided it into sections and paragraphs;
I fear this may violate the Holy Intent or erroneously judge right and wrong. I pray that you, both the hidden and the manifest, will illuminate this and know that all is as it is.

Although one must repent, if one clearly contemplates the Dharma, one must realize that it is "mind-only. Relying on the teachings and following the masters, the lineage begins with the Patriarch Nāgārjuna and is transmitted through the sacred scriptures to Nanyue and Tiantai.
In the past, Nanyue and Tiantai together received the Buddha’s direct teaching at Vulture Peak;

now, in this life, they have personally awakened to it, wondrously harmonizing with the site of enlightenment. They illuminate the Lotus Sūtra like the high sun shining upon a deep valley, reaching full understanding.
All phenomena resemble the long wind wandering through the great void; arising from stillness, one attains meditative concentration and realizes the *dhāraṇī* that encompasses all.

One simultaneously awakens to the dharma-gates of both the Great and Small Vehicles. These words are true and sincere; I dare not transmit them falsely. Diligently relying on contemplation and diligently practicing cultivation, one responds by ascending to the fruits of sainthood.

Within a single thought-moment, the three thousand realms are complete, encompassing both the environment and its inhabitants. Object and contemplation are non-dual. Through the six stages and ten levels, the paths differ yet remain one.
May all beings, their minds purified, ascend to the other shore; may they contemplate and cultivate the causes, practicing them as the seeds of Bodhi.

Whether in accordance with or contrary to [the path], may all return to liberation. Wherever the cause of liberation may lie, may one use the power of supernormal knowledge and wisdom to lead others to abide therein.
May those who have not yet proclaimed it always joyfully request its teaching, and may those who have already studied it revere it as the Buddha.
I exhort those who have not yet studied to give rise to the aspiration; may the void have its limits, but this vow be inexhaustible. May this mind remain thus forever in the future.
In the present, throughout the four modes of conduct, may I never for a moment be separated from it. In this life and in other realms, may I always hear the Buddha-dharma.
May all beings within the dharma-realm—whether enemies or kin—participate equally in this ocean of vows.
Record of the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* (End).

On the eighteenth day of the sixth month, the Jǐwèi cycle, in the year Dīngyōu of the Yuánhé era (1197), the old monk Xíngmǎn of Tiantái, while at Cānlín Monastery, happened upon this manuscript; he personally transcribed it with his own hand out of reverence.
It is the constant way of antiquity that the Dharma is revered and its people esteemed. Master Cōng resided long at the Vihāra, where we together listened to a single school of teaching;

as we inherited this tradition, seeing things now makes us reflect upon the man, and our feelings of grief and joy arise together. I, Mǎn, being a mere student who has received the teachings at the end of the line, see this record and clearly perceive the subtle contemplation (*miào guān*) of Tiantai.
As the ancients said: "The wise know wisdom, and the snake knows itself. This is truly so.

The true vehicle (saddharmayāna) is complete in a single thought-moment; who knows that the environment and its inhabitants, cause and effect, are all of one suchness, and that the three thousand realms arise from emptiness and the provisional?
This is the unique teaching of our own school. When later students behold this, it may serve as a seed for the vehicle.

Even those who slander it will be like the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging—nothing will ever be in vain. I pray you will hear of this wondrous contemplation. After a hundred years, I, the old monk, shall give full testimony. All together... [end of fragment].
The commentary and notes were recorded and preserved at Fulong Monastery.

On the twenty-third day of the third month in the twelfth year of the Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty, at the Yelao Su Yuan of Kaiyuan Monastery in Taizhou, the scribe-monk Zhou Jing transcribed this.
On the twenty-fifth day, it was verified by a Japanese monk.
The Bhikṣu Yuanzhen respectfully records that he has read this alongside his seniors, wishing for their high aspirations to endure forever.
